title: Observable Estimation in the Absence of Classical Verification
authors: Samantha V. Barron, Bradley Mitchell, Vinay Tripathi, Francesco Grieco, Ilan Rosen, Francesca Pietracaprina, Davide Materia, Alireza Seif, Darvin Wanisch, Ramón L. Panadés-Barrueta, Ewout van den Berg, Jay-U Chung, Andrew Eddins, Sam Ferracin, Guillermo García-Pérez, John Goold, Luke C. G. Govia, Holger Haas, Ian Hincks, Jesse C. Hoke, Zoë Holmes, Su-un Lee, Youngseok Kim, Swarnadeep Majumder, Sabrina Maniscalco, Simone Montangero, Daniel Puzzuoli, Tomaž Prosen, James Raftery, Ricardo Rivera Cardoso, Max Rossmannek, Manuel Rudolph, Brendan Saxberg, Liran Shirizly, Karthik Siva, Joshua Skanes-Norman, Ilaria Siloi, Kevin C Smith, Boris Sokolov, Maika Takita, Yanting Teng, Mao Tian Tan, Joseph Tindall, Zoltán Zimborás, Matteo A. abstract: The predictive success of quantum mechanics underpins many areas of modern science, even as the exact simulation of large, interacting quantum systems remains beyond the reach of classical computation. This success has been enabled by the remarkable advancement of scalable numerical approximation methods, which often demonstrate practical accuracy despite the absence of formal guarantees. As quantum simulation pushes into regimes where these approximations struggle, a fundamental challenge arises: How can quantum outcomes be trusted when reliable classical benchmarks are unavailable? Here, we establish a framework for the independent validation of quantum estimates in this setting and present evidence that they provide the most credible result among several considered methods, in the absence of an immediately accessible ground-truth solution. We apply our framework to the semi-scrambling dynamics of a physical model that strains several leading classical simulation methods yet remains experimentally accessible, in part through our introduction of the \textit{operator Loschmidt echo}. We systematically design a series of experiments using quantum heuristics that, taken together, test the underlying assumptions and provide strong confidence in the observable estimates obtained from the quantum computer. We then show how this framework can be extended to place accuracy bounds on quantum estimates via careful characterization and manipulation of the device noise, transforming the problem of validating the observable estimation to validating the noise model. These results establish a route towards trusted quantum computation for scientific discovery, independent of classical verification.
summary: This paper presents a novel framework to validate quantum estimates of physical observables when exact classical verification is impossible. By applying this to semi-scrambling dynamics on superconducting qubits, the authors demonstrate methods that rely on internal consistency checks or precise noise model characterization rather than external ground truths. This establishes a crucial pathway toward trusted quantum computation for scientific discovery.
main_problem: The core challenge is establishing a reliable method for validating quantum estimates of physical observables when direct, exact classical benchmarks are unavailable due to computational limitations.
main_result: The authors establish a framework using consistency checks or by rigorously characterizing the noise model (e.g., via PEC) to build confidence in quantum results independent of classical ground truth.
method: They combine theoretical frameworks for error bounding (like Probabilistic Error Cancellation, PEC) with experimental measurements on superconducting hardware, utilizing advanced diagnostics like the operator Loschmidt echo.
model_or_system: The study applies this framework to semi-scrambling dynamics of a heterogeneous Floquet Ising model simulated on a 56-qubit section of a heavy-hex lattice using superconducting transmon qubits.
key_observables: Operator Loschmidt echo (OLE) signal ($	ext{S}_\delta$), expectation values, and error rates for various gate types.
important_parameters: Scattering strength ($\eta$), perturbation strength ($\delta$), circuit depth ($L$), and Pauli error rates ($\lambda_P$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve the validity of noise models (e.g., assuming $\delta$-independence for global rescaling) and the ability to accurately characterize hardware noise channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate circuit diagrams for OLE computation, compare error rates across different gate types, show how classical heuristics diverge from quantum results at intermediate parameters, and detail overhead reduction achieved by advanced error mitigation techniques like SLC.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the need for validation beyond classical benchmarks to applying this framework using the OLE on a complex physical model. It then details sophisticated noise characterization methods (PEC/SLC) before concluding with tests of observable sensitivity across sub-lattices.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the 'trustworthiness' bottleneck in quantum simulation, providing concrete protocols for validating results when classical theory breaks down—a critical concern for AMO and open quantum systems research.

FIG. 4. Loschmidt echo: The Loschmidt echo can be visualized as evolving from an initial object (state or observable) under a certain unitary W, and back propagation with a perturbed Wδ. (a) In the absence of perturbation, the initial condition is exactly recovered. (b) Perturbation leads to a mismatch between the initial and final states or observables. (c) In this experiment Wδ = UVδ, so the perturbation is localized in time, in the middle of the echo dynamics.
